difficultyRationale: A basic but commonly-misunderstood mechanic of consumer-group scaling in Kafka.
prompt: A topic has 4 partitions. A team scales its consumer group from 4 instances up to 6, expecting higher throughput. What actually happens to the 2 extra consumer instances?
explanation: Within one Kafka consumer group, each partition is assigned to at most one consumer instance at a time, and a topic with 4 partitions can therefore keep at most 4 consumer instances in that group actively reading. The 2 extra instances receive no partition assignment at all and sit idle — they consume nothing — until either the partition count is increased or some of the other 4 instances leave the group.

options.text: The 2 extra instances are assigned the same partitions as 2 of the original 4, so each of those partitions ends up being read redundantly by two consumers at once, doubling throughput on those two partitions specifically without affecting the other two.
options.explanation: A partition is assigned to at most one consumer within a given group at a time; Kafka does not let two consumers in the same group read the same partition concurrently, so there is no redundant doubled reading.

options.text: A topic with 4 partitions can have at most 4 actively-consuming instances in one consumer group; the 2 extra instances receive no partition assignment and sit idle until the partition count increases or other instances leave.
options.explanation: Correct. Partition count is the hard ceiling on parallelism within a single consumer group — adding consumers beyond that count doesn't increase throughput, it just leaves the excess instances unassigned and idle.

options.text: Kafka automatically splits each of the 4 existing partitions into 2 sub-partitions internally, so the new instance count of 6 maps cleanly onto 8 effective partitions without any manual repartitioning needed.
options.explanation: Kafka partitions are not automatically split at runtime to accommodate more consumers; the partition count of a topic is fixed unless an administrator explicitly increases it, and doing so does not retroactively reorganize existing data into new partitions cleanly.

options.text: The group coordinator rejects the 2 extra instances' join requests outright, so they fail to start up and the application reports a consumer group join error rather than silently running idle in the background.
options.explanation: The extra instances successfully join the consumer group and participate in its protocol; they are simply left without any partitions assigned by the rebalance, which is a silent idle state, not a join failure or rejected connection.

references.title: Confluent Documentation — Kafka Consumer Design ("Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer within each consumer group at any given time")
